###### **_#inclusion #access_** As in the previous edition of this Report, the percentage of adults with relationships with financial institutions3 remained above 85% during this period, reaching 96% in 2020. This high percentage is partly due to the inclusion of all accounts still open, even those with very low balances or that have not registered any withdrawals, deposits, and transfers for long periods. Based on information provided by the financial institutions themselves, data disclosed by the Banco Central do Brasil (BCB) unveil the universe of account holders registered in the National Financial System (SFN). By contrast, the survey _O brasileiro e os hábitos de uso de meios de pagamento_ (Brazilians and their habits of using the means of payment),4 conducted by the BCB in 2019, pointed out that 77% of adults maintained a relationship with the SFN. Between 2018 and 2020, there were great diversification in the types of institutions used by the population, with a significant increase in the share of payment institutions (IPs). The number of relationships with IPs grew 179%, while, considering the entire SFN, the growth was 49% in this period, as shown in Figure 1.1.1. **Figure 1.1.1 – Individuals’ relationships with the SFN by segment****5** 300

Its intensive use, despite the short period of existence, indicates that the Brazilian population, in general, has been very receptive to the new means of payment. **Access to the SFN** , which had already been at high levels, expanded in 2020, with the inclusion of 14 million citizens in the system. With this, 96% of the adult population in Brazil established some kind of financial relationship. In addition to this most recent expansion of access, the past analysis showed that the **diversification of providers** has changed the landscape of institutions that provide financial services to the Brazilian citizen, especially the IPs, which were responsible for about 30% of the new relationships established in the analyzed period. 

Regarding **products and services** , in the last three years the population with some credit operation increased slightly reaching, by the end of 2020, almost 50% of the adult population in Brazil. From the income perspective, the use of credit reflects the country's inequality, as 50% of the population with the lowest income have approximately 12% of the credit portfolio balance in 2020. 

When analyzing the use of **digital financial services** , it was possible to look into a scenario of increasing digitalization. Even the lower income groups have increasingly sought relationships with IPs, which focus heavily on offering digital financial services. These groups also increasingly adopted Pix in the very first months after its implementation. The migration to digital occurs even in a scenario where income is configured as the main barrier for Brazilians to access the Internet and digital means of payment. 

The year 2020 could not be overlooked in the **analysis of recent developments** , a period strongly marked by the **impacts of the Covid-19 pandemic on financial citizenship** . Besides driving greater digitalization of financial services, the conditions imposed by the pandemic also had effects on other aspects of Brazilians' financial lives. The first effect was the expanded access, with an increase of almost 10% in the number of people in Brazil maintaining a relationship with the SFN, from 149 to 163 million in 2020. A relevant part of this expansion seems to be related to the Federal Emergency Aid, a benefit that may also be related to the more expressive drop in delinquencies specifically in that year.

The five types of Pix keys are: (1) email address, (2) mobile phone number, (3) CPF, (4) CNPJ, and (5) random key (a random set of characters generated by the system). Finally, **looking to the future** , the RCF highlighted **innovations** that have the potential to change the way financial services are offered. In this sense, it was observed that IPs have gained relevance in the financial lives of citizens, with their customer portfolio increasing from fifteen million in 2017 to sixty million in 2020. A second group of institutions with potential to impact financial citizenship, especially in the expansion of access to and use of credit, began operating in the SFN in this triennium were the SPEs and the SCDs, both known as credit fintechs. 

Besides the new institutions, specific innovations in the regulatory and payment environment brought important implications for financial citizenship: (i) **Open Banking** , which enables a scenario of greater competition, diversification and customization and tends to make services cheaper, more conveniently accessed by customers and better suited to the profile, needs and objectives of each person; (ii) the **Regulatory Sandbox** , which also fosters the creation of innovative products and services and has among its strategic priorities to encourage the emergence of financial and payment solutions with potential effects of stimulating financial inclusion and fostering credit for micro-entrepreneurs and small businesses; and (iii) the launch of **Pix** operation, which was conceived by BCB to facilitate the lives of citizens and companies, whether payers or payees. Pix seeks to enable new business models, reduce costs, contribute to the digitalization of means of payment and provide financial inclusion. 

The adoption of Pix, for example, was fast, and the **digitalization of means of payment with impacts on digital financial inclusion** also seems to have occurred on the very first months of operation. By August 2021, around forty million citizens who previously did not use electronic means of payment began to do so through Pix, which demonstrates effects beyond a simple change to other digital means of payment. 

These nuances in the analysis of **financial citizenship** show how this subject has advanced in recent years and highlight the various challenges yet to be overcome. The constant monitoring of this reality is essential for developing new technologies and innovative solutions and adequately evaluating their consequences on the lives of citizens and their relationship with the SFN.

The growth of new IPs accounts might have been associated to the search for remote access channels during the pandemic. This search also seems to have occurred by the low-income population who already maintained a relationship with financial institutions. Chapter 3 brings further details about IPs’ operations. The implementation of Pix has a great potential to boost digital financial inclusion In November 2020, BCB launched the Pix,37 with a potential to democratize the access to electronic payment services in the country and encourage even further the delivery of financial digital services to the lowincome population (see an analysis about the Pix in chapter 3). A few months after its implementation, data concerning the use of Pix by the low-income population already show the potential of change. In March 2021, 34.9% of the adult population in the _CadÚnico_ had already registered at least one Pix key, 21.4% had already sent a Pix transfer, and 24.6% had already received one (Figure 1.2.7). This figure shows data for the _Bolsa Família_ beneficiary groups and individuals registered in the _CadÚnico_ not benefited by the Program, as well as the remaining Brazilian adult population (not registered in the _CadÚnico_ ), for the sake of comparison. > 36 In Figure 1.2.6, “Other Segments” includes credit unions, specialized banks, credit institutions, and capital markets.

Regarding **products and services** , in the last three years the population with some credit operation increased slightly reaching, by the end of 2020, almost 50% of the adult population in Brazil. From the income perspective, the use of credit reflects the country's inequality, as 50% of the population with the lowest income have approximately 12% of the credit portfolio balance in 2020. When analyzing the use of **digital financial services** , it was possible to look into a scenario of increasing digitalization. Even the lower income groups have increasingly sought relationships with IPs, which focus heavily on offering digital financial services. These groups also increasingly adopted Pix in the very first months after its implementation. The migration to digital occurs even in a scenario where income is configured as the main barrier for Brazilians to access the Internet and digital means of payment. The year 2020 could not be overlooked in the **analysis of recent developments** , a period strongly marked by the **impacts of the Covid-19 pandemic on financial citizenship** . Besides driving greater digitalization of financial services, the conditions imposed by the pandemic also had effects on other aspects of Brazilians' financial lives. The first effect was the expanded access, with an increase of almost 10% in the number of people in Brazil maintaining a relationship with the SFN, from 149 to 163 million in 2020. In this sense, it was observed that IPs have gained relevance in the financial lives of citizens, with their customer portfolio increasing from fifteen million in 2017 to sixty million in 2020. A second group of institutions with potential to impact financial citizenship, especially in the expansion of access to and use of credit, began operating in the SFN in this triennium were the SPEs and the SCDs, both known as credit fintechs. Besides the new institutions, specific innovations in the regulatory and payment environment brought important implications for financial citizenship: (i) **Open Banking** , which enables a scenario of greater competition, diversification and customization and tends to make services cheaper, more conveniently accessed by customers and better suited to the profile, needs and objectives of each person; (ii) the **Regulatory Sandbox** , which also fosters the creation of innovative products and services and has among its strategic priorities to encourage the emergence of financial and payment solutions with potential effects of stimulating financial inclusion and fostering credit for micro-entrepreneurs and small businesses; and (iii) the launch of **Pix** operation, which was conceived by BCB to facilitate the lives of citizens and companies, whether payers or payees. Pix seeks to enable new business models, reduce costs, contribute to the digitalization of means of payment and provide financial inclusion. The adoption of Pix, for example, was fast, and the **digitalization of means of payment with impacts on digital financial inclusion** also seems to have occurred on the very first months of operation. By August 2021, around forty million citizens who previously did not use electronic means of payment began to do so through Pix, which demonstrates effects beyond a simple change to other digital means of payment. These nuances in the analysis of **financial citizenship** show how this subject has advanced in recent years and highlight the various challenges yet to be overcome.
